q: What is the version skew policy between Helm and Kubernetes, and why does it matter?
a: Helm releases state which Kubernetes minor versions each Helm minor version supports, typically the cluster version it was built against and a few versions behind. Helm talks to the API server using client libraries compiled for a specific Kubernetes version, so using a very old client against a new cluster can fail on removed APIs or miss features, and a very new client against an old cluster may send fields the server rejects. The practical rule is to keep Helm within the supported range for the clusters you manage, pin the Helm version in CI so every environment uses the same client, and upgrade the client when clusters upgrade. Charts add their own constraint with the kubeVersion field in Chart.yaml, which makes Helm refuse an install on unsupported clusters. During Kubernetes upgrades, I check deprecated and removed APIs in installed releases before upgrading the control plane, since Helm cannot upgrade a release whose stored manifests use a removed API without the mapkubeapis plugin. Documenting the supported matrix prevents surprises across teams.
f: Why pin the Helm version in CI?
What does the kubeVersion field do?
p: Each Helm minor supports a range of Kubernetes versions, so pin Helm in CI, upgrade it with clusters, set kubeVersion in charts and check releases for removed APIs before upgrading the control plane.
tip: Say pin the client; check removed APIs before cluster upgrades.

q: How do you inspect an installed release with helm status, get, history and show?
a: Several commands reveal different parts of a release. Helm list shows releases, namespaces, revisions, status, chart and app version, and with the all-namespaces and all flags includes failed and uninstalled ones. Helm status prints the current status, the resources and the rendered notes text, which often contains connection instructions. Helm get has subcommands: values shows the user-supplied values, with the all flag adding computed ones; manifest shows the exact YAML that was applied; hooks shows hook resources; notes shows the notes; and all combines them. Helm history lists every revision with its status and description, which shows when failures happened, and helm diff revision compares two revisions. Helm show, by contrast, inspects a chart, not a release: it prints the chart metadata, readme and default values. When troubleshooting, I compare the manifest of the working revision with the failing one, and compare the effective values with the values files in Git to detect drift between what is deployed and what was intended.
f: What is the difference between get values and show values?
How do you find when a release started failing?
p: Use helm list, status, get values/manifest/hooks/notes and history to inspect a release, and show to inspect a chart. Compare revisions with the diff plugin and check effective values against Git.
cmds: helm get manifest app -n prod --revision 7 > r7.yaml
tip: Say get is for releases; show is for charts.

q: How do namespaces work with Helm releases, and what does --create-namespace do?
a: A Helm release lives in a namespace, and its record is stored there as a secret. The namespace flag chooses where the release is installed and where namespaced resources are created, unless a template explicitly sets another namespace in metadata. The same release name can exist in different namespaces, which is how one chart is deployed per environment or tenant. The create-namespace flag creates the target namespace if it does not exist, which is convenient for development, but the namespace Helm creates is not part of the release and has no labels, quotas, network policies or pod security settings. In governed clusters, namespaces are created separately by a platform process with those controls, and the pipeline's role may not have permission to create them. A chart that hard-codes namespace in templates breaks this model, so templates should use the release namespace value. Cluster-scoped resources in a chart are not namespaced, and their names should include the release to avoid collisions. Uninstalling a release does not delete the namespace.
f: Why avoid hard-coded namespaces in templates?
Does uninstall remove the namespace?
p: Releases and their records live in a namespace; use the release namespace value in templates, prefer platform-created namespaces with quotas and policies over --create-namespace in production, and name cluster-scoped resources with the release to avoid clashes.
tip: Say namespaces are governed by platform, not by helm flags.

q: What is the difference between helm lint, helm template and helm install --dry-run?
a: They validate at different depths. Helm lint examines the chart structure and templates for errors and warnings, such as invalid Chart.yaml, missing required fields, template syntax problems and values schema violations, without needing a cluster, and the strict flag turns warnings into failures. Helm template renders the templates locally with the supplied values and prints the manifests, using default capabilities unless told otherwise, with no cluster connection; it shows exactly what would be applied, and its output can be piped to validators like kubeconform. Helm install or upgrade with dry-run renders and then contacts the API server for validation, which can detect issues such as unknown kinds, admission rejections and lookups of existing objects, but still does not create anything. With debug, it prints the computed values and manifest. A good pipeline uses all three: lint for chart quality, template plus schema validation and policy checks for rendered output, and server-side dry run before production deployment to catch cluster-specific problems, followed by the diff plugin for change review.
f: Which of these needs cluster access?
Why use the strict flag?
p: Lint checks chart structure and templates offline, template renders manifests locally for validation, and dry-run adds server-side checks through the API without creating anything. Use all three plus diff in a pipeline.
tip: Say lint the chart, template the output, dry-run the cluster.

q: When would you choose a Kubernetes operator instead of a Helm chart to manage an application?
a: A Helm chart renders and applies manifests once per install or upgrade and then stops; it has no ongoing logic. An operator is a controller that runs continuously, watches custom resources and reconciles real state toward the desired state, encoding operational knowledge such as backups, failover, scaling, upgrades with ordering and health checks. For stateless applications and simple configuration, a chart is usually enough, being simpler to write, review and audit. For complex stateful systems like databases, message brokers and clusters, where lifecycle tasks go beyond creating objects, an operator is a better fit, because it can react to failures and perform multi-step procedures safely. Many projects combine both: a chart installs the operator and its CRDs, and users then create custom resources to declare instances. The trade-offs are that operators add components to run, secure and upgrade, introduce their own APIs to learn, and bugs in them can affect many workloads. I choose operators for mature, well-maintained ones, and avoid writing my own unless the lifecycle logic justifies the engineering cost.
f: What does a chart not do after install?
How do charts and operators combine?
p: Charts apply manifests and stop; operators continuously reconcile and encode operational logic such as backups and failover. Use charts for stateless and simple apps, operators for complex stateful systems, and often a chart to install the operator.

q: How do you generate several resources from a list in values, for example multiple CronJobs or Ingress hosts?
a: Rather than copying a template for each resource, I define a list or map in values and use range in the template to render one resource per entry. A single file can contain multiple YAML documents separated by triple dashes, and the range loop emits a separator and a full resource for each item. Inside the loop the dot refers to the current item, so I use the dollar sign or a variable captured earlier to reach release metadata and helper templates. For maps, range gives the key and value, with the key naturally used for naming; I sort keys so output order is stable. Names should combine the release fullname and the item name and respect the length limit. Optional per-item fields get defaults, and a required call guards mandatory ones. Validation through the values schema helps users catch mistakes. This pattern suits workers, scheduled jobs, additional ports, extra volumes and multiple ingress rules. For very different resources, separate templates remain clearer, and over-generic loops can make templates hard to read.
f: Why use the dollar sign inside the loop?
How do you keep output order stable?
p: Define a list or map in values and range over it in one template, emitting a document separator and a resource per item, using $ for root context, combined names, defaults and required fields. Use schema validation and keep loops readable.
tip: Say one template, many resources, via range.

q: How do you load and use files inside a chart with .Files, Files.Glob, AsConfig and AsSecrets?
a: The Files object gives templates access to non-template files packaged with the chart, except those excluded by the helmignore file and files in the templates directory. Files.Get returns the content of a single file as a string, which is ideal for embedding a script or configuration into a ConfigMap, and Files.GetBytes returns bytes. Files.Glob returns a set of files matching a pattern, and the AsConfig method turns them into key-value pairs suitable for the data section of a ConfigMap, with file names as keys; AsSecrets does the same with base64 encoding for secrets. Lines and Lines iterate content. Files can also be passed through tpl to evaluate template expressions within them, giving templated configuration files stored as real files, which editors handle better than long strings in YAML. Limits to remember: the whole chart is stored in the release record, so large files inflate it and can hit size limits; and binary or sensitive files should not be bundled. Paths are relative to the chart root.
f: What does AsConfig produce?
Why avoid large files in charts?
p: Files.Get reads one packaged file, Files.Glob selects many and AsConfig or AsSecrets turn them into ConfigMap or Secret data; run through tpl if they contain expressions. Avoid large or sensitive files because the chart is stored in the release record.
tip: Say real files beat giant YAML strings.

q: How do you use semverCompare, fail and NOTES.txt to make a chart helpful and safe?
a: Charts can protect users and guide them. The semverCompare function compares version strings against constraints, typically comparing Capabilities.KubeVersion.Version with a range, so a template can pick the correct apiVersion or refuse unsupported combinations, and the same can validate the application version. The fail function aborts rendering with a custom message, which is the right way to stop on invalid combinations that a schema cannot express, such as enabling autoscaling together with a fixed replica count or specifying both an existing secret and an inline password, producing a clear error instead of a confusing result. The required function is a shorter form for a missing value. The NOTES.txt file in templates is rendered after install and upgrade and shown to the user: it explains how to reach the application, get the generated password from a secret, port-forward for access, and warns about important next steps or deprecations. It can use the same templating and conditionals, for example showing different instructions for ingress or load balancer exposure. Good messages reduce support questions and misconfiguration.
f: When use fail instead of a schema?
What goes into NOTES.txt?
p: Use semverCompare for version-aware templates, fail with clear messages for invalid combinations a schema cannot express, required for mandatory values, and NOTES.txt to show access instructions, secrets retrieval and warnings after install.
tip: Say fail early with a message that explains the fix.

q: Which string, list and dictionary functions from Sprig do you use for safe name and label handling?
a: Names and labels have strict rules, so Sprig helpers are essential. Trunc cuts a string to a length, usually 63, and trimSuffix removes a trailing hyphen after truncation. Replace changes characters, for instance turning a plus sign in a chart version into an underscore for labels. Lower, upper, title and kebabcase normalise case. Printf builds strings with formatting, and join, split and splitList convert between lists and strings. Regex functions such as regexMatch and regexReplaceAll validate or clean input. For lists, first, last, append, concat, uniq, sortAlpha and has support manipulation, and for dictionaries, dict creates a map to pass multiple arguments into an included template, merge and mergeOverwrite combine maps, keys and values list contents, hasKey tests existence, pick and omit select entries, and deepCopy avoids mutating shared data. Sha256sum, b64enc and b64dec support checksums and encoded secrets. I wrap commonly used combinations in named templates so the same logic produces consistent names everywhere, and I keep expressions short enough to read.
f: How do you pass several values to an included template?
Why wrap name logic in helpers?
p: Use trunc and trimSuffix for 63-character limits, replace for illegal characters, printf and join for building strings, dict to pass multiple arguments to includes, merge and hasKey for maps, and sha256sum or b64enc for checksums and secrets. Wrap common logic in helpers.
tip: Say wrap fiddly logic in one helper.

q: How do you write a template that merges user-supplied annotations, labels or env vars with chart defaults without duplicates?
a: Users expect to add their own metadata and environment variables while the chart keeps required defaults. For maps such as labels and annotations, I build the final map with merge or mergeOverwrite, combining the chart's standard labels, those from a global value, and the user's extra labels, and then render it with toYaml. The order determines precedence, and I make sure user values cannot override selector labels, because selectors must stay stable. A helper template returns the merged map so every resource uses it consistently. For environment variables, which are lists in Kubernetes, merging is harder: I either expose a map in values and convert it to a list in the template, sorted by name, or accept an extra list that is appended to the defaults, and warn that duplicates produce undefined behaviour. The envFrom field handles bulk injection from config maps and secrets. Templates should handle empty values gracefully with default and with blocks. Documentation lists which keys are reserved. Tests check that defaults survive and overrides apply as expected.
f: Why protect selector labels?
How do you convert an env map into a list?
p: Use merge or mergeOverwrite in a helper to combine standard labels, global values and user extras, render with toYaml, keep selector labels immutable, convert env maps to sorted lists or append extra lists, and test that defaults survive and overrides apply.
tip: Say merge into one map; never touch selectors.

q: How do you document chart values so users know what each option does?
a: Values are the user interface, so documentation must be close to the code and kept current. In values.yaml, each key has a comment above it describing purpose, type, default and allowed values, written in a consistent format that tools can parse. The helm-docs tool reads these comments, including special annotations for type and description, and generates a readme table automatically, run in a pre-commit hook or CI so the readme never drifts from the file. The values schema adds machine-readable types, enumerations and descriptions, and editors use it for auto-completion and validation. The readme also includes installation instructions, prerequisites, upgrade notes between versions, common configuration examples such as a production values file, and how to configure ingress, persistence and secrets. Artifact Hub displays the readme and can show the values schema. A changelog in the chart records new, renamed and removed values, which helps users upgrade. Examples that are tested in CI ensure that documented configurations actually render, avoiding stale instructions.
f: How does helm-docs generate tables?
Why test the examples?
p: Comment each key in values.yaml in a parseable format, generate the readme table with helm-docs in pre-commit or CI, add a values schema, document upgrades and examples, keep a changelog of renamed or removed values and test that examples render.
tip: Say generate the table; don't hand-write it.

q: How should image tags and digests be handled in chart values?
a: Images are the most frequently changed value, so the design should be both convenient and safe. Common values are repository, tag and pull policy, with the tag defaulting to the chart's appVersion when empty. Pipelines override the tag at deploy time or, better, commit the new tag to the environment's values file so it is traceable. Mutable tags such as latest or a branch name are risky because different nodes can pull different content and rollbacks are unreliable, so I use immutable version tags or digests. A digest reference, with the sha256 value, pins exact content and protects against tag overwrites or registry compromise; the template renders repository at digest when a digest value is provided, otherwise repository colon tag. Pull policy should be IfNotPresent for versioned tags and Always only when tags are mutable. For multiple containers, init containers and jobs, the same pattern applies, ideally through a shared helper that builds the image string with an optional global registry prefix. This supports mirroring to internal registries. Admission policies enforce no latest tags and approved registries.
f: Why prefer digests?
How does a global registry prefix help?
p: Expose repository, tag, digest and pullPolicy; default the tag to appVersion, avoid mutable tags, prefer digests, build image strings in a shared helper with an optional global registry prefix for mirrors, and enforce with admission policy.
tip: Say immutable tags or digests, one helper.

q: How do you size resources and autoscaling per environment using values without duplicating whole files?
a: Environments differ mainly in scale, so only those settings should differ between values files. The base file sets modest defaults that work anywhere, and each environment file overrides replica counts, resource requests and limits, autoscaling bounds and storage sizes. Presets can reduce errors: a value such as size set to small, medium or large maps in a helper to resource blocks, with an explicit resources value taking precedence for exceptions. Autoscaling values include enabled, minimum, maximum and target utilisation, and the template omits fixed replicas when it is enabled. Requests are based on measured usage from monitoring, with vertical pod autoscaler recommendations as input, and limits are set carefully because CPU limits can cause throttling while memory limits protect nodes. Pod disruption budgets and topology spread settings are scaled with the replica count. Production values are reviewed with capacity in mind, and quota in namespaces enforces ceilings. A rendered diff between staging and production shows that only intended scale-related values differ. Load tests validate the sizing before it reaches production.
f: Why omit replicas with HPA?
How are requests chosen?
p: Keep a modest base values file and override only scale settings per environment, optionally with size presets, omit replicas when autoscaling is on, base requests on measured usage and VPA advice, scale PDBs and spread constraints, and diff rendered environments.
cmds:
# values/prod.yaml
resources:
  requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}
autoscaling:
  enabled: true
  minReplicas: 4
  maxReplicas: 20
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 65
tip: Say thin overrides: only scale differs.

q: How do you deploy the same chart for many tenants or customers safely using values?
a: Multi-tenant deployments multiply configuration, so structure and automation matter. One approach is a release per tenant, each in its own namespace, with a small values file containing only tenant-specific settings such as hostname, sizing, feature toggles and external identifiers, layered over shared defaults. A generator reads a tenant list and produces the releases: a GitOps ApplicationSet or Flux Kustomization with templating, or a Helmfile with a loop. Isolation comes from namespaces, resource quotas, network policies and separate secrets, with credentials per tenant stored in an external secret manager. Upgrades roll out in waves, internal tenants first, then small ones, then large, with health checks and the ability to hold back a tenant on an older chart version if it needs more time. Data per tenant is separated physically or logically as the application requires. Observability labels metrics and logs with the tenant. Onboarding and offboarding are automated, including deletion of data. A schema validates tenant files, and a rendered diff for sample tenants is reviewed on changes. Avoid copy-pasting values for hundreds of tenants.
f: Why roll out in waves?
How are tenants isolated?
p: Create a release and namespace per tenant with small tenant values over shared defaults, generate them with ApplicationSets, Flux or Helmfile, isolate with quotas, network policies and per-tenant secrets, upgrade in waves, label observability by tenant and validate files with a schema.
cmds:
generators:
  - git:
      repoURL: https://git.example.com/platform/tenants
      files:
        - path: "tenants/*.yaml"
tip: Say generate tenants; don't copy them.

q: How do you use JSON Schema conditionals and references in values.schema.json for stronger validation?
a: A basic schema checks types and required fields, but JSON Schema also supports conditions and reuse that capture real constraints. The if, then and else keywords make fields required only when another is set, for example requiring a host and TLS secret name when ingress is enabled, or requiring a storage size when persistence is on. The oneOf and anyOf keywords express alternatives, such as providing either an inline password or an existing secret name but not both. Definitions with $ref reuse structures like a resources block or an image block in several places, keeping the schema short and consistent. Patterns validate formats like DNS names, durations and quantities, and enumerations restrict choices. Setting additionalProperties false at key levels catches typos in key names, though it should be omitted where users may add arbitrary keys, such as annotations. Helm validates against draft-07 and reports errors with the path, so messages are useful. Tests render the chart with valid and invalid example values to confirm the schema rejects what it should. The schema is maintained with the chart, and tools can generate a starting version.
f: How do you require fields only when a feature is enabled?
Why use additionalProperties false?
p: Use if/then/else to require fields when features are enabled, oneOf for exclusive alternatives, $ref definitions for reuse, patterns and enums for formats, and additionalProperties false to catch typos where appropriate. Test valid and invalid values against the schema.
tip: Say schemas can express dependencies, not just types.

q: How do you add init containers, sidecars and extra volumes to a chart in a flexible way?
a: Applications often need extra containers: an init container to wait for a dependency or fetch configuration, a sidecar for log shipping, a proxy or certificate reloader, and extra volumes and mounts for secrets or shared files. A good chart exposes these as values so users can add them without forking: lists such as initContainers, extraContainers, extraVolumes and extraVolumeMounts, rendered with toYaml and the tpl function when values need templating, for example referencing the release name. The chart documents the format as standard Kubernetes container specs. The main container's own mounts and the shared emptyDir volumes for sidecar communication are defined in the template, and security context defaults apply to additional containers too, which is where charts often forget. Resource requests for sidecars matter because they count toward pod scheduling. With native sidecar support in recent Kubernetes versions, init containers with a restart policy of Always give sidecars proper start-up and shutdown ordering. Probes, termination ordering and log collection are tested together, since sidecars can block pod termination or readiness.
f: Why does tpl help with extra containers?
What do native sidecars improve?
p: Expose initContainers, extraContainers, extraVolumes and extraVolumeMounts as values rendered with toYaml and tpl, apply security defaults and resource requests to extras, document the format and use native sidecars for better ordering on recent Kubernetes.
tip: Say expose extension points instead of forcing forks.

q: How do you template Ingress and Gateway API resources in a chart across different controllers?
a: Traffic exposure varies widely between clusters. For Ingress, the chart exposes enabled, class name, annotations, hosts with paths and path types, and TLS entries with secret names, rendering the correct apiVersion for the cluster. Annotations are controller-specific, so they are passed through rather than hard-coded, and the ingress class uses the ingressClassName field instead of the deprecated annotation. Certificates are usually obtained through cert-manager by adding an issuer annotation. The service port can be referenced by name to avoid mismatches. For the newer Gateway API, the chart may render HTTPRoute resources referencing an existing Gateway through parent references, with hostnames, matches, filters and backend references, leaving the shared Gateway to the platform team. Offering both, behind separate enabled flags, eases migration. Defaults keep exposure off or internal, because accidental public exposure is a security risk. Tests render combinations, validate against API schemas and check that hosts and TLS settings line up. NOTES.txt tells users the URL. Multi-host and path-based routing patterns come from list values iterated with range.
f: Why pass annotations through instead of hard-coding?
What does HTTPRoute reference?
p: Expose enabled, class, annotations, hosts, paths and TLS for Ingress, pass controller annotations through, support cert-manager, optionally render Gateway API HTTPRoute referencing a platform Gateway, default to no public exposure and test combinations.
tip: Say pass controller specifics through; default to private.

q: How do you template PodDisruptionBudgets, HorizontalPodAutoscalers and topology spread correctly in a chart?
a: These resources protect availability and scale, but they interact, so the chart must be careful. A PodDisruptionBudget limits voluntary disruptions during node drains and upgrades; the chart exposes minAvailable or maxUnavailable, never both, and renders it only when enabled and the replica count makes it meaningful, since a budget requiring one available pod with a single replica blocks node drains forever. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler references the deployment, with min and max replicas and metric targets, and the deployment template omits the replicas field when it is enabled. Resource requests must be set for CPU-based scaling to work. Topology spread constraints and pod anti-affinity spread replicas across nodes and zones; the chart provides defaults using the selector labels with a soft preference, so scheduling still succeeds in small clusters, and allows overrides. Selector labels in all of them must match the pods exactly. Values for these are validated, and unit tests render combinations such as autoscaling on with the budget enabled. Documentation explains the interactions and recommended production settings.
f: Why can a PDB block node drains?
How do the HPA and replicas field interact?
p: Expose minAvailable or maxUnavailable (not both) for PDBs and avoid budgets that block drains with a single replica; omit replicas when the HPA is enabled; provide soft topology spread defaults using selector labels; require resource requests and test combinations.
tip: Say availability objects must match selectors and replicas.

q: How do you handle Jobs and CronJobs in a chart, including migrations, ttl and history settings?
a: Jobs run to completion and are immutable once created, which causes upgrade problems when a chart templates a job with the same name. Options are to use a hook with a delete policy so the job is recreated for each release, to add a unique suffix such as the revision or a checksum to the name so each upgrade creates a new job, or to set ttlSecondsAfterFinished so completed jobs clean themselves. Migration jobs usually run as pre-upgrade hooks with a backoff limit, an active deadline and resource limits, and they must be idempotent. CronJobs expose schedule, time zone, concurrency policy of Allow, Forbid or Replace, starting deadline, history limits for successful and failed jobs, suspend and the job template. Forbid is the safe default when overlap would be harmful. The chart should set a restart policy of OnFailure or Never, and the pod spec shares the security context and image helper with other workloads. Failures should alert through metrics or logs, not rely on someone looking at history. Time zones and daylight changes need care, and jobs must tolerate being run twice.
f: Why are Jobs a problem on upgrade?
What does concurrencyPolicy Forbid do?
p: Jobs are immutable, so recreate them with hooks and delete policies, unique names or ttlSecondsAfterFinished. Give migrations backoff and deadlines; for CronJobs expose schedule, time zone, concurrencyPolicy Forbid by default, history limits and suspend, and make work idempotent.
cmds:
spec:
  schedule: {{ .Values.cron.schedule | quote }}
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
      backoffLimit: 2
tip: Say jobs are immutable; recreate them deliberately.
